name: Agricultural Drones: Data Analytics and Precision Agriculture
objectives: Given a stitched drone map and its processing report, check the map's position accuracy and image quality and report the error, using check points or a stated method, before any analysis
Given a crop, its growth stage and the camera used, choose a vegetation index and explain why it fits, and confirm it against the true-colour map and the ground
Using QGIS and an index map, create zones and report each zone's area and mean index, and count plants or trees, with counts checked on a ground sample and the error reported
Given zones and their ground-truthed causes, build a prescription map with a rate or task for each zone, using two to four rates taken from soil tests or local recommendations
For a proposed precision action, calculate a partial budget with a cautious and a likely case, counting only what changes, and saying honestly if it does not pay
For a farmer or estate manager, write a short result that leads with the action, in their language and units, showing how sure you are and what was checked on the ground

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Is the map accurate enough to act on?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a drone map's position accuracy and image quality before analysing it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a stitched drone map and its processing report, you will check the map's position accuracy and image quality and report the error, using check points or a stated method, before any analysis.
Before you send workers to a zone, you need to trust that the map puts things in the right place. A drone's ordinary GNSS can place a map a few metres off. That is fine for finding a wet corner, but not for guiding work to single rows or matching maps from different dates.
Three ways to improve and check accuracy: ground control points (GCPs), marked targets on the ground whose coordinates you measure with an accurate GNSS receiver and use in processing; drones with RTK or PPK positioning, which correct position during or after the flight; and check points, extra measured targets not used in processing, used to test the final map. Report the error you measured.
Also check quality: the processing report (how many images were used, any warnings), the real image detail (GSD), blur, holes and stitching errors. For maps you will compare over time, use the same method each time and make sure they line up on top of each other.
Step by step:
- Read the processing report: images used, warnings, GSD.
- Look for blur, holes and stitching errors.
- Measure position error at check points (or compare with known features).
- Decide whether the accuracy fits the decision.
- For time series, check that maps line up.
Words to know:
- Ground control point (GCP): a marked ground target with accurately measured coordinates, used to fix a map's position.
- RTK / PPK: methods that correct drone positions during (RTK) or after (PPK) the flight for high accuracy.
- Check point: a measured target used only to test a map's accuracy.
- Processing report: the summary the stitching software produces about a map's quality.
Official sources:
- OpenDroneMap (free, open-source drone mapping software)
Try it now: Open the processing report of a map you made (or a sample dataset's report). Write down the number of images used, the GSD, any warnings, and decide whether the map is accurate enough to (a) find wet areas, (b) guide replanting of single rows.
You can now check a drone map's accuracy and quality and decide whether it fits the decision.

check.q: What are check points used for?
options: Testing the final map's accuracy, because they are not used in processing
check.why: Check points are extra measured targets kept out of processing, so you can measure the map's real error.

check.q: You will compare this month's map with last month's to guide work in single rows. What do you check first?
options: That both maps are accurate and line up on top of each other
Nothing; ordinary GNSS is always enough
check.why: Ordinary GNSS can be a few metres off, so maps used for rows or over time must be accurate and aligned.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing the right vegetation index
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a vegetation index that fits the crop, stage and camera.
This lesson builds toward: Given a crop, its growth stage and the camera used, you will choose a vegetation index and explain why it fits, and confirm it against the true-colour map and the ground.
NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) is the best-known index; FAO uses it from satellites to track vegetation across Africa. But NDVI tends to saturate in dense, healthy canopies such as mature maize, tea or coffee: values bunch up near the top and small differences disappear.
NDRE uses the red-edge band instead of red: (NIR - RedEdge) / (NIR + RedEdge). It stays sensitive in dense canopies and often shows nitrogen and chlorophyll differences later in the season. With only a colour camera, indices such as VARI, (Green - Red) / (Green + Red - Blue), or Excess Green, 2 x Green - Red - Blue, separate green plants from soil and show rough vigour; they are useful for stand and weeds but less reliable for stress.
Choose by the question: early-season stand and weeds, an RGB index or NDVI; mid-season vigour in open crops, NDVI; dense canopies and nitrogen, NDRE. Whatever you choose, look at the true-colour map too, and confirm on the ground.
Words to know:
- Saturation: when an index stops changing even though plants still differ, as NDVI does in dense canopies.
- Red edge: a narrow band of light between red and near-infrared, sensitive to chlorophyll.
- NDRE: Normalized Difference Red Edge index, more sensitive than NDVI in dense canopies.
- VARI: Visible Atmospherically Resistant Index, a vegetation index from RGB bands only.
Official sources:
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (NDVI and vegetation indicators)
- QGIS (free, open-source GIS)
Try it now: For each case choose an index and write why: (a) stand count in 3-week-old maize with an RGB drone, (b) nitrogen differences in a closed tea canopy with a multispectral drone, (c) mid-season vigour in cassava with a multispectral drone.
You can now choose a vegetation index that fits the crop, its stage and the camera.

check.q: Why can NDVI miss small differences in mature maize, tea or coffee?
options: It saturates in dense, healthy canopies
check.why: In dense, healthy canopies NDVI values bunch up near the top, so small differences disappear.

check.q: You have only an RGB camera and want to see crop stand early in the season. Which index do you choose?
options: An RGB index such as VARI or Excess Green
check.why: RGB indices separate green plants from soil and suit early-season stand and weeds.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Zonal statistics and counting in QGIS
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Measure each zone's area and average index, and count plants or trees.
This lesson builds toward: Using QGIS and an index map, you will create zones and report each zone's area and mean index, and count plants or trees, with counts checked on a ground sample and the error reported.
Analysis turns a coloured map into numbers people can act on. First, create zones: classify the index map into classes (for example low, medium, high), then turn them into polygons and tidy away tiny fragments; or draw zones by hand with the farmer's knowledge. Calculate each zone's area.
Then use QGIS Zonal Statistics to calculate, for each zone, the mean, minimum, maximum and spread of the index. Compare zones, and compare the same zones over dates. A table such as Zone A: 3.2 ha, mean NDVI 0.71; Zone C: 0.8 ha, mean NDVI 0.48 is much easier to act on than a picture.
Counting: for tree crops (avocado, mango, coffee), tree crowns are often clear on high-detail RGB maps and can be counted by hand with points, or with plugins and scripts. For row crops, count in sample plots and scale up. Always check a sample of counts on the ground and report the error.
Step by step:
- Classify the index map into a few classes, or draw zones with the farmer.
- Convert classes to polygons; remove tiny fragments; calculate area.
- Run Zonal Statistics for mean, min, max and spread per zone.
- Count trees or plants (points, plugin or sample plots).
- Check counts on the ground and report the error.
Words to know:
- Zonal statistics: numbers (such as average) calculated for the pixels inside each zone.
- Polygon: a closed shape on a map, such as a zone or field boundary.
- Classify: group pixel values into a few classes, such as low, medium and high.
Official sources:
- QGIS (free, open-source GIS)
Try it now: In QGIS with your map or a sample: draw or classify three zones, calculate their areas, run Zonal Statistics on the index, and make a table of zone, area and mean value. If it is a tree crop, count trees in one zone.
You can now measure zones and count plants or trees in QGIS and present the results as a table.

check.q: What does a zone statistics table give you?
options: Numbers such as each zone's area and mean index
check.why: Zonal statistics turn a coloured map into numbers people can act on.

check.q: Your software counted 1,240 avocado trees. What do you do before reporting it?
options: Check a sample of counts on the ground and report the error
check.why: Counts are checked on a ground sample and the error is reported.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a prescription map
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn zones into a prescription map with a rate or task for each zone.
This lesson builds toward: Given zones and their ground-truthed causes, you will build a prescription map with a rate or task for each zone, using two to four rates taken from soil tests or local recommendations.
A prescription map tells a machine or a worker what to do in each zone. Start from the cause, not the colour: use ground-truthing and, where possible, soil tests to learn why each zone differs. Then choose an action per zone: more or less fertilizer, a different seed rate, replanting, drainage, weeding, or no change.
Rates come from agronomy, not from the drone. Use soil test results and local recommendations from your national research institute or extension service for the crop and area. The map only says where each rate goes. Keep the number of rates small (two to four) so it is practical.
For machines, export the zones as a shapefile or the format the controller accepts. For hand application, print or share a simple zone map with each zone's instruction in grams per planting hole or bags per zone, and mark zones in the field. Spray or spread prescriptions applied by drone need the aviation and pesticide approvals your country requires.
Step by step:
- Confirm the cause in each zone (ground-truthing, soil tests).
- Choose an action per zone.
- Take rates from soil tests and local recommendations.
- Keep two to four rates.
- Export for machines, or make a printed zone map with instructions for workers.
Words to know:
- Prescription map: a map that tells a machine or worker how much to apply, or what to do, in each zone.
- Shapefile: a common GIS file format for zones and boundaries.
- Soil test: a laboratory analysis of soil nutrients and acidity.
Official sources:
- FAO and WHO: Guidance for aerial application of pesticides (2024)
- QGIS (free, open-source GIS)
Try it now: Using your three zones from Lesson 3, write a prescription table: zone, area, likely cause, action, rate (marked "from local recommendation" if you do not have one), and how workers will find the zone.
You can now build a practical prescription map with a rate or task for each zone.

check.q: What does a prescription map show?
options: What to apply or do in each zone
check.why: A prescription map tells a machine or worker what to do in each zone.

check.q: A zone looks weak on the map. What do you do before choosing an action?
options: Find the cause by ground-truthing and, where possible, a soil test
check.why: Start from the cause, not the colour; the action depends on why the zone differs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Does it pay? A simple partial budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out whether a precision action pays using a partial budget.
This lesson builds toward: For a proposed precision action, you will calculate a partial budget with a cautious and a likely case, counting only what changes, and saying honestly if it does not pay.
A partial budget compares only what changes. On one side: extra income (more yield sold) and money saved (less fertilizer where it was wasted). On the other: extra costs (drone service, more input in some zones, labour) and income lost. If the first side is bigger, the change pays.
Example with placeholder numbers in Kenya shillings: a 4-hectare maize farm pays KSh 6,000 for mapping. The prescription moves 2 bags of fertilizer from a 1-hectare waterlogged zone, where it was wasted, to a 2-hectare average zone, so no extra fertilizer is bought, and the farmer expects 5 extra bags of maize from that zone. Benefit: 5 bags x the local price per bag. Costs: KSh 6,000 for mapping + the labour to dig a drain by hand. Use real local prices and a cautious yield estimate.
Show a range, because yield and price vary: a cautious case and a likely case. Also count the benefits that are hard to price, like earlier warning of fall armyworm. Be honest if the numbers do not pay on a small farm; a cooperative or shared service may change the answer.
Step by step:
- List extra income and money saved.
- List extra costs and income lost.
- Use local prices and cautious yield estimates.
- Calculate a cautious case and a likely case.
- Write the answer honestly, with what could change it.
Words to know:
- Partial budget: a simple comparison of only the costs and benefits that change when you change one thing.
- Break-even: the point where extra benefits just equal extra costs.
Try it now: Do the partial budget for the example using real prices from your local market (maize price per bag, fertilizer price per bag, labour per day). Calculate a cautious case (3 extra bags) and a likely case (5 extra bags). Does it pay?
You can now use a partial budget to show whether a precision action pays.

check.q: In a partial budget, which counts as a cost?
options: The fee for the drone mapping service
A higher price for the harvest
check.why: Extra costs such as the drone service and labour go on the cost side.

check.q: Your likely case pays, but your cautious case loses money. What do you tell the farmer?
options: Both cases honestly, with what drives the difference
check.why: Yield and price vary, so you show a range and are honest when the numbers are close.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Communicating results so farmers act
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Present analysis results in a short, clear form a farmer will act on.
This lesson builds toward: For a farmer or estate manager, you will write a short result that leads with the action, in their language and units, showing how sure you are and what was checked on the ground.
The best analysis is wasted if the farmer does not understand or trust it. Lead with the answer and the action: "Zone C (the low corner by the road, about 2 acres) is waterlogged. Dig a drain before topdressing. Do not add fertilizer there this season." Then show the map with zones in simple colours and familiar landmarks.
Use the channel and language the farmer uses: a printed page, a picture and short message on WhatsApp or SMS, or a voice note in Kiswahili, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or another local language. Use local units (acres, bags, debes) as well as hectares and kilograms. Keep numbers few.
Show how sure you are, and what was confirmed on the ground. Offer to walk the field together. Agree what will be checked next time, and record what the farmer did, so the next analysis can show whether it worked. Keep farmers' data private and share only with their permission.
Step by step:
- Write the answer and action first, zone by zone.
- Show a simple map with landmarks.
- Use the farmer's channel, language and units.
- Say how sure you are and what was confirmed.
- Agree a follow-up and record what the farmer did.
Words to know:
- Landmark: a feature people know, such as a road, tree, store or river, used to find places.
- Follow-up: a later check to see if the action worked.
Official sources:
- FAO and ITU: E-agriculture in Action: Drones for Agriculture (2018)
Try it now: Final task: complete your analysis and write the one-page farmer result: accuracy and how checked, the index and why, the zone table and count, the prescription map, the partial budget, and plain-language actions with a follow-up date.
You can now deliver drone analysis as clear, trusted actions a farmer can follow.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Map accuracy No accuracy stated, or no quality check. The map's accuracy and how it was checked are stated, with image quality checked in the processing report. Uses check points and reports the measured error. Index choice The index is not justified, or does not fit the crop or camera. The index fits the crop, stage and camera, with a short reason. Compares two indices and shows why one was chosen. Zones and counts No zone statistics, or counts are not checked. Each zone's area and mean index, and a plant or tree count checked on a ground sample. Compares the same zones over two dates. Prescription map Rates are guessed or there are too many rates. Two to four rates or tasks per zone, from local recommendations, linked to ground-truthed causes. Exported in a format the machine or workers can use. Partial budget No budget, or it counts things that do not change. A partial budget with a cautious and a likely case using local prices. Notes benefits that are hard to price and when a shared service would help. Farmer's result Longer than one page or starts with technical detail. One page that leads with the action, in plain language and local units, with how sure you are. Prepared in the farmer's own language and channel, with a follow-up check agreed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the analysis and check it again.

check.q: How should a farmer's result start?
options: With the answer and the action to take
check.why: Leading with the answer and the action helps the farmer act on it.

check.q: The farmer reads Kiswahili and uses WhatsApp. How do you send the result?
options: A long English PDF by email
Nothing; tell the estate office only
A picture of the zone map with a short message or voice note in Kiswahili
check.why: Use the channel and language the farmer uses, with few numbers and local units.
